questions.q: Which type of necrosis occurs in the brain after infarction?
questions.exp: Brain tissue has high lipid and minimal collagen — neutrophil enzymes liquefy it, producing cystic cavities.

questions.q: Coagulative necrosis is typical of:
questions.exp: Coagulative necrosis preserves tissue architecture for several days after ischaemic injury (e.g. MI, kidney infarct).

questions.q: Caseous necrosis is characteristic of:
questions.exp: Caseous necrosis ('cheese-like') is seen in TB granulomas and certain systemic fungal infections.
optExp: DVT is thrombus, not necrosis type per se.

questions.q: Fat necrosis with saponification (chalky white areas) is classically seen in:
questions.exp: In acute pancreatitis, lipase digests fat → free fatty acids + Ca²⁺ form chalky saponified deposits.

questions.q: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in:
questions.exp: Immune complexes deposit in vessel walls causing fibrin-like material accumulation and necrosis (e.g. malignant HTN, polyarteritis nodosa).

questions.q: Wet gangrene differs from dry gangrene in that wet gangrene:
opts: Secondary bacterial infection with tissue liquefaction
questions.exp: Wet gangrene involves bacterial superinfection leading to liquefactive necrosis with foul odour. Dry gangrene is purely ischaemic.
optExp: Diabetes is a risk factor but not exclusive.

questions.q: Apoptosis differs from necrosis in that apoptosis:
opts: Programmed, organized cell death without inflammation
Releases cell contents into surrounding tissue
questions.exp: Apoptosis is energy-requiring, programmed cell death without inflammation. Necrosis is messy and inflammatory.
optExp: Apoptotic bodies are phagocytosed; cytoplasmic content is retained.

questions.q: Which is NOT a type of cell adaptation?
questions.exp: Apoptosis is cell death, not adaptation. Adaptations include hypertrophy, hyperplasia, atrophy, metaplasia, dysplasia.

questions.q: Metaplasia refers to:
opts: Reversible change from one differentiated cell type to another
Disordered growth with loss of normal architecture
questions.exp: Metaplasia is the reversible conversion from one adult cell type to another (e.g. Barrett's oesophagus: squamous → columnar).

questions.q: Dysplasia is characterised by:
opts: Disordered growth with loss of normal architecture
questions.exp: Dysplasia features atypical cells (loss of differentiation, irregular nuclei), but the basement membrane is intact — pre-cancerous.

questions.q: Hypertrophy of the cardiac left ventricle in response to hypertension is an example of:
opts: Increase in the number of cardiac myocytes
Increase in size of individual cardiac myocytes
Replacement of cardiac muscle with another cell type
questions.exp: Cardiac myocytes cannot divide; LV hypertrophy is purely cell enlargement, not increased cell number.

questions.q: The 5 cardinal signs of inflammation include all EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Cardinal signs: rubor (redness), calor (heat), dolor (pain), tumor (swelling), functio laesa (loss of function). Necrosis is a tissue change, not a cardinal sign.

questions.q: Which mediator primarily causes vasodilation and increased vascular permeability in acute inflammation?
questions.exp: Multiple mediators contribute, but histamine is the immediate/early mediator, with bradykinin, leukotrienes, NO, and cytokines amplifying.
optExp: Major systemic effects but not the most immediate.

questions.q: The correct order of leukocyte extravasation is:
questions.exp: Margination (edge), rolling (selectins), firm adhesion (integrins), diapedesis (out into tissue).

questions.q: Granulomas are characteristic of:
questions.exp: Granulomas form when macrophages cannot eliminate the antigen — chronic inflammation with epithelioid macrophages, multinucleated giant cells.
optExp: Some viral infections produce granulomas but not typical of viral hepatitis.

questions.q: Which cell type predominates in granulomas?
questions.exp: Granulomas are dominated by activated macrophages (epithelioid cells) and multinucleated giant cells, with surrounding lymphocytes.

questions.q: A non-caseating granuloma is most characteristic of:
questions.exp: Non-caseating granulomas are characteristic of sarcoidosis. Caseating granulomas are typical of TB.
optExp: Hepatitis B/C are not classic granuloma diseases.

questions.q: Which cytokine is a major pyrogen and is targeted by anti-inflammatory biologics in RA?
questions.exp: TNF-α is a key pyrogen and inflammatory cytokine, blocked by drugs like infliximab in rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.q: Chronic inflammation is characterised by infiltrate of:
questions.exp: Chronic inflammation involves mononuclear cells (lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages) with possible fibrosis and granuloma formation.

questions.q: A benign tumour of glandular epithelium is termed a(n):
questions.exp: -oma denotes benign; adenoma = benign glandular tumour. Carcinoma denotes malignant epithelial.
optExp: CIS is dysplasia confined to epithelium.

questions.q: A malignant tumour of mesenchymal origin is a:
questions.exp: Sarcomas arise from mesenchymal tissue (bone, muscle, fat, fibrous, blood vessels). Carcinomas are epithelial.

questions.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of malignant (not benign) tumours?
opts: Invasion of surrounding tissues and metastasis
questions.exp: Invasion past the basement membrane and metastasis define malignancy.

questions.q: Anaplasia describes:
opts: Increase in the number of cells
questions.exp: Anaplasia = lack of differentiation, with disorganised cells and bizarre nuclei — a hallmark of malignancy.

questions.q: Carcinoma in situ refers to:
opts: Malignant epithelial cells confined within the basement membrane
Metastatic carcinoma that has spread to distant sites
Benign tumor with slow growth pattern
Granulation tissue forming at wound sites
questions.exp: CIS has high-grade dysplasia involving full thickness of epithelium but has not breached the basement membrane.
optExp: CIS is more advanced than inflammation.

questions.q: Most common route of metastasis for sarcomas is:
opts: Direct invasion into adjacent tissues only
questions.exp: Sarcomas typically spread via blood (haematogenous, often to lung). Carcinomas typically spread via lymph first.

questions.q: A cervical smear showing abnormal epithelium with atypia but intact basement membrane is:
opts: Hyperplasia with increased cell numbers but normal appearance
Metaplasia with replacement by different cell type
Dysplasia with cellular atypia but intact basement membrane
Carcinoma in situ with breach of basement membrane
Invasive carcinoma with spread to surrounding tissues
questions.exp: Dysplasia is abnormal cellular features without breach of basement membrane. CIS is full-thickness dysplasia.
optExp: Hyperplasia is increased number, not atypia.
CIS is more severe but related (full-thickness).
Invasive carcinoma has broken through basement membrane.

questions.q: Virchow's triad components are:
opts: Endothelial injury, blood stasis, and altered blood composition
Pain, swelling, and redness at affected site
Platelets, fibrin, and red blood cells
Pressure changes, flow alterations, and time duration
questions.exp: Virchow's triad: endothelial injury, abnormal flow (stasis/turbulence), hypercoagulability — predisposing factors for thrombosis.

questions.q: A 60-year-old woman immobilised after surgery develops DVT. The MOST contributing Virchow's factor is:
questions.exp: Immobilisation reduces venous return, causing stasis — the predominant factor for post-operative DVT.
optExp: Surgery can cause some injury, but stasis predominates here.
Surgery and inflammation can contribute, but stasis is key.
Not the dominant factor in DVT.

questions.q: A young man with fractured femur develops respiratory distress and petechial rash. Which embolism?
opts: Fat embolism from bone marrow release
questions.exp: Fat embolism syndrome: fat from marrow enters bloodstream after long-bone fractures → respiratory distress, petechiae, cerebral symptoms 24-72 h later.
optExp: Thromboembolism does not classically cause petechiae.

questions.q: Air embolism most commonly occurs:
questions.exp: Air can enter circulation during surgery, central line insertion, or scuba diving (decompression).

questions.q: Pulmonary embolism most often arises from thrombi in the:
opts: Deep veins of the lower limbs
questions.exp: Most PEs originate from DVTs in deep veins of the lower limbs, traveling through right heart to lungs.
optExp: Renal artery emboli go to kidney.

questions.q: The coagulation cascade ultimately generates which protein to form a clot?
opts: Fibrinogen protein in its inactive form
Fibrin generated by thrombin from fibrinogen
Von Willebrand factor for platelet adhesion
questions.exp: Thrombin (IIa) cleaves fibrinogen to fibrin monomers, which polymerise to form the clot mesh.
optExp: Thrombin is the enzyme; fibrin is the product.

questions.q: The first step of thrombus formation at site of vascular injury is:
questions.exp: Endothelial injury exposes collagen; platelets adhere via vWF and GPIb, then activate and aggregate.
optExp: Fibrin formation is later in cascade.

questions.q: Reversible cell injury features include:
opts: DNA fragmentation in a patterned manner
questions.exp: Hallmarks of reversible injury: cellular swelling (hydropic change), fatty change, and ribosome detachment. Necrosis features are irreversible.

questions.q: Apoptosis is regulated by:
questions.exp: Caspases are cysteine proteases that execute apoptosis (initiator caspases 8/9 → effector caspases 3/6/7).
optExp: NO is involved in macrophage killing but not the executioner.

questions.q: Pus is a mixture of:
questions.exp: Pus is purulent exudate composed of dead/dying neutrophils, tissue debris, and oedema fluid.
optExp: Bacteria may be present but not alone.
Lymphocytes dominate chronic, not acute pus.

questions.q: Resolution after acute inflammation is most likely when:
questions.exp: Complete resolution occurs when injury is limited and tissue stem cells can regenerate normal architecture.

questions.q: Oncogenes:
opts: Silent genetic mutations with no effect
questions.exp: Oncogenes (e.g. RAS, MYC) are activated proto-oncogenes; one mutated copy can drive uncontrolled growth.
optExp: Tumour suppressors are different (e.g. p53, Rb).
TSGs are recessive at cellular level.

questions.q: Tumour suppressor genes (e.g. p53, Rb):
opts: Activated and overexpressed in cancer cells
Lost or inactivated in both alleles (two-hit hypothesis)
questions.exp: Knudson's two-hit hypothesis: both alleles of a TSG must be inactivated. p53 is mutated in >50% of cancers.

questions.q: Atrial fibrillation predisposes to thromboembolism mainly via:
opts: Blood stasis in the left atrial appendage
questions.exp: Loss of coordinated atrial contraction leads to stasis (especially in left atrial appendage), promoting thrombus formation → stroke risk.
optExp: Possible in some but not classic AF.

questions.q: An infarct in the brain typically heals by:
questions.exp: CNS neurons cannot regenerate; necrotic tissue liquefies, leaving a fluid-filled cyst surrounded by gliosis (astrocyte scar).
optExp: Most other organs use coagulative + fibrosis.

questions.q: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis has chronic joint inflammation with pannus formation. The predominant infiltrate is:
questions.exp: RA is chronic autoimmune inflammation with mononuclear cell infiltrate, immune complex deposition, and synovial hyperplasia.
optExp: Neutrophils dominate acute inflammation, not RA pannus.

questions.q: A pregnant woman in labour suddenly develops respiratory distress, hypotension, and DIC. Most likely:
questions.exp: Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare but catastrophic complication of labour, presenting with sudden cardiorespiratory collapse and DIC.

questions.q: Free radicals damage cells primarily through:
questions.exp: ROS (e.g. superoxide, H₂O₂) oxidise membrane lipids, proteins, and DNA, causing cell injury and death.

questions.q: Endogenous antioxidants include all EXCEPT:
questions.exp: NADH is a reducing equivalent but not an antioxidant. Glutathione, SOD, catalase, vitamins C/E are antioxidants.

questions.q: Cachexia in cancer is mediated mainly by:
questions.exp: Cancer cachexia involves TNF-α, IL-6, and other cytokines that increase catabolism and reduce appetite.

questions.q: Bradykinin in inflammation causes:
opts: Causes vasodilation and increased vascular permeability with pain
questions.exp: Bradykinin causes vasodilation, vascular permeability, and is a potent mediator of pain. ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin → cough.

questions.q: Heparin's mechanism of action is:
opts: Activates antithrombin III to enhance thrombin inhibition
questions.exp: Heparin binds antithrombin III, accelerating its inactivation of thrombin (IIa) and factor Xa.

questions.q: Warfarin acts by:
opts: Inhibits vitamin K-dependent clotting factor synthesis
questions.exp: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X (and proteins C/S).

questions.q: Common sites for metastatic cancer to spread are:
questions.exp: Common metastatic sites are lung, liver, bone (especially axial), and brain — reflecting blood flow and microenvironment.
optExp: Skin is uncommon as primary site.
Pancreatic mets are not the typical pattern.

questions.q: Lipofuscin pigment in cells indicates:
opts: Accumulation of indigestible cellular debris from normal wear and tear
Pathological calcium deposition in cardiac tissue
questions.exp: Lipofuscin is a yellow-brown 'wear and tear' pigment from oxidised membrane lipids, accumulating in long-lived cells (heart, neurons, liver).
